I've been farming this same land in Quzhou for 20 years. I know what this soil wants, what the wells can give, and what prices look like come harvest. My husband works in the county town now, so I'm managing most of the field work myself with help from my mother-in-law during busy periods. That means I have to be practical — I can't afford to chase fancy methods that cost more labor than I have.

**My thinking, crop by crop:**

**Wheat and maize** are my bread and butter. They go on the same 7 mu, winter wheat then summer maize. For wheat, I'll use the Jimai variety my neighbors have been using — it yields steadily and the village supply co-op carries it. I'll rotary till after maize harvest in October, apply base fertilizer, and plant in mid-October. I'll irrigate at sowing, before winter sets in, at jointing, and before heading — four times total if the spring is dry like last year. For maize after wheat harvest in June, I go straight no-tillage — no time to properly plough and still catch the rains, and honestly the yields have been fine. Hybrid seed, Zhengdan 958 or whatever the township agricultural station recommends this year. Two irrigations if needed.

**Cotton** goes on the remaining 3.1 mu. Cotton is a lot of work — spraying for bollworm and whitefly alone takes many days — but the cash income is good and my mother-in-law can help pick. I'll do a rotary till in spring before transplanting seedlings in late April. I apply more fertilizer to cotton and irrigate through boll development. Five pesticide rounds is usually what it takes here.

I won't switch to anything unfamiliar this year. Stable inputs, standard practices I trust. If wheat prices are low at harvest I'll hold some in the grain bin.
